newsitem.title: UK: Britain seeks to boost mature North Sea oil acreage.
newsitem.headline: Britain seeks to boost mature North Sea oil acreage.

text.p: Britain expects to announce next year a 'free for all' oil licensing round in which all unlicensed areas of the North Sea will be put up for grabs, energy minister Lord Fraser said on Tuesday.

"New licensing initiatives proposed today ensure one of our greatest industrial success stories of recent decades maintains its impetus into the 21st century," Lord Fraser told oil industry representatives in London.

The proposal to open up all North Sea acreage in an 18th licensing round, designed to renew exploration interest in mature offshore acreage, is just one of the recommendations of a government review launched in July amid concerns over the extent of fallow acreage in the North Sea.
An open licensing round would put two thirds of the U.K. North Sea, or some 800 blocks, under the hammer, Lord Fraser said.
"I want this to be the round of ideas," said Lord Fraser. "We'll take a much more open approach and see how much interest this excites."
The 18th licensing round is expected to be launched by November next year, while a programme of further rounds, probably at yearly intervals, should also be announced in 1997.
The review also recommends open access across all licensed acreage for seismic surveys.

"I expect the regulations for the future 18th offshore round will remove licensees' exclusive right of access for surveying," Lord Fraser said. "Open seismic access is a major encouragement to innovative analysis."
After consultation with the industry, Lord Fraser said he doubted that U.S.-style cash bidding would become the standard method for allocating acreage in the North Sea.

"Auctioning acreage does not speed up exploration," he said. "It does not reduce cycle times...In fact some companies use the cash bidding system to bank acreage without much intention of working it at all."
At present, companies win North Sea licenses by promising to carry out certain seismic and drilling work.
But Lord Fraser said that while the this "obligatory work" system will remain dominant, sealed cash bids may be used in certain circumstances and the idea will be "left on the table".
The review also makes recommendations to build on the results of the fallow field initiative launched in March, which looked at acreage which has not been drilled for six years.
Out of the 115 blocks identified as fallow, activity is now planned on 72 blocks, including 23 wells, while nine news wells have been drilled since March, Lord Fraser said.
"In future we shall take steps to discourage licence holders from letting their acreage languish under-explored or with undeveloped discoveries," he said.
These steps could include taking into account oil companies' track records in awarded new licenses, or rent increases to encourage companies to relinquish unproductive acreage, he said.

The new proposals relating to mature areas of the North Sea will not affect West of Shetlands acreage to be awarded in the 17th round, or the licensing of other frontier areas such as the "White Zone" currently in dispute with the Faroe islands, Lord Fraser said.
Junior Energy Minister Richard Page announced on Tuesday that regulations for the 17th round are now in effect, and companies will soon be able to apply for licenses.
